note: Phase 1 source audit. Every field was checked against the primary source unless a limitation says otherwise. 'unknown' means not determinable from public materials as of the audit date.

sources.title: Teens, Social Media and AI Chatbots 2025
sources.population: U.S. teens ages 13-17 who live with their parents
sources.samplingMethod: Online survey via Ipsos KnowledgePanel (probability-based, address-based sampling); teens recruited through panelist parents; weighted by age, gender, race/ethnicity, household income and other categories; Black and Hispanic oversamples
aiUseVariables: specific chatbots used (ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta AI, Copilot, Character.ai, Claude)
sources.microdataNote: Same survey wave as the Feb 2026 report. Not listed on pewresearch.org/datasets as of 2026-10-07. Pew releases case-level data 'after a period of time'; recheck periodically.
limitations: Self-reported use; no behavioral logs
Excludes teens not living with a parent
Cross-sectional; first year the broad chatbot question was asked, so no trend
Too few Asian teens for separate analysis

sources.title: How Teens Use and View AI
sources.population: U.S. teens ages 13-17 who live with their parents, and their parents
sources.samplingMethod: Same survey as pew-2025-12 (Ipsos KnowledgePanel, probability-based, weighted). External IRB review (Advarra).
aiUseVariables: share of schoolwork done with chatbot help
cognitionVariables: open-ended reasons AI will harm society, coded (incl. 'overreliance, loss of critical thinking or creativity')
decisionMakingVariables: whether AI would do better/worse than people at tasks (diagnosis, hiring, etc.)
sources.microdataNote: Not yet released as of 2026-10-07. When released, it would allow within-survey cross-tabs (e.g., schoolwork reliance x confidence x demographics) but contains no measured cognitive or learning outcome.
limitations: Many items asked only of chatbot users (n=894) or schoolwork users (n=766); bases must be tracked
'Overreliance / critical thinking' appears only as a coded open-end among teens expecting a negative societal impact (n=354) - a perception, not a measure
No measure of critical thinking, idea generation, or learning outcomes

sources.title: Teens in the AI Era: Schoolwork and Skills That Matter
sources.organization: Common Sense Media (data collection: NORC at the University of Chicago)
sources.samplingMethod: Hybrid: 682 from NORC AmeriSpeak Teen (probability panel; cumulative response rate 11.7%) + 335 nonprobability interviews from Prodege (quota-based), combined via NORC TrueNorth calibration and raked to 2026 CPS totals
sources.marginOfError: +/- 4.3 percentage points (combined sample, incl. design effect)
sources.representativeNote: Described as nationally representative, but one-third of the sample is nonprobability and relies on model-based calibration. Treat as representative with a weaker footing than Pew.
aiUseVariables: AI tool types used for schoolwork
ways AI is used (answer as-is / rewrite / improve; brainstorm / check / feedback)
learningVariables: AI makes me a more successful student
feel I miss out on learning
cognitionVariables: I come up with fewer of my own ideas because AI is available
aiLiteracyVariables: teacher ever discussed: AI safety, how AI works, judging AI accuracy
sources.microdataNote: No public dataset found. Questionnaire is published.
limitations: Attitude items (66%, 51%, 39%, 38%) are among teens who use AI for schoolwork (n=665), not all teens
Self-reported perceptions, not measured cognition or learning
Hybrid probability/nonprobability sample
Press release states 27% of teens had discussed safe AI use with a teacher; the report body says 30% (27% is the share for 'what AI is and how it works'). This audit uses the report.
Skills comparison by AI use (e.g., fact checking 31% vs 19%) is inconsistent with the overall 50% on the same item; not used until clarified

sources.title: More Students Use AI for Homework, and More Believe It Harms Critical Thinking: Selected Findings from the American Youth Panel
sources.fieldDates: 2025-12-04 to 2026-01-05 (with Feb 2025 and May 2025 comparison waves)
sources.population: U.S. youth ages 12-29 enrolled in middle school (grades 5-8), high school (grades 9-12), or undergraduate/trade postsecondary
sources.samplingMethod: RAND American Youth Panel (subset of the probability-based RAND American Life Panel); weighted to enrolled youth by gender, race/ethnicity, grade level, region. Earlier waves added Ipsos KnowledgePanel members; May 2025 oversampled CA, FL, NY, TX.
aiUseVariables: uses AI help for homework (none / 1-2 classes / 3+ classes)
learningVariables: whether each use counts as cheating
cognitionVariables: agreement: 'The more students use AI for their schoolwork, the more it will harm their critical thinking skills'
sources.microdataNote: RAND ran a respondent-level multivariate regression itself (AI homework use on critical-thinking belief, school rules, teacher checking, cheating worry; controls for grade and gender). Public access to AYP microdata not confirmed; RAND Survey Panels should be contacted.
limitations: Headline figures (62%, 67%) pool middle school, high school and college; use the high-school subgroup for teen claims
Critical-thinking item measures a belief about students in general, not the respondent's own critical thinking
Trend waves differ in eligibility (ages 12-21 vs 12-29) and panels; RAND did not test trends for significance
Regression is correlational; RAND states it cannot identify causes
High-school subgroup values below were read from chart labels in the PDF and need a second check

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Public Feedback Survey - What We Heard
sources.population: Self-selected respondents reacting to draft NYCPS AI guidance (educators, parents/families, students, school leaders, community members)
sources.samplingMethod: Anonymous open online survey (Alchemer link) promoted via NYCPS channels. NYCPS states it was not a scientific sample and responses may include duplicates.
cognitionVariables: concern: 'Cognitive development (AI doing the thinking students should do)'
sources.microdataNote: Aggregates only; 3,300+ open-ended comments reviewed by NYCPS but not published.
limitations: Not representative of NYC students, parents, or educators
Educators (47%) and parents/families (44%) dominate; student share not verified in this audit
Possible duplicate responses
Measures concern about a draft policy, not student behavior
Per-group column order in the concerns table must be checked manually before any group values other than parents and community members are used

sources.title: NYC Public Schools AI policy timeline (guidance, delay, K-8 moratorium)
sources.organization: NYC Public Schools press release; Chalkbeat New York; ABC News
sources.population: Policy documents and reporting, not survey data
limitations: Moratorium details come from news reporting (ABC News, 2026-09-02); confirm against an official NYCPS document before publishing
Policy is not evidence of effects on students

sources.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
sources.organization: Bastani et al., Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122(26)
sources.population: High school math students at one school in Turkey
sources.ageRange: high school (ages not stated in abstract)
sources.sampleSizeNote: 'Nearly a thousand' students per the abstract; exact N to be taken from the paper
sources.samplingMethod: Randomized field experiment: GPT Base (ChatGPT-like) vs GPT Tutor (learning safeguards) vs no access
limitations: Not U.S.; one school; one subject; short intervention
Measures math learning, not critical thinking
Supports a causal claim about a specific tool design in a specific setting, not about AI use in general

sources.title: About a quarter of U.S. teens have used ChatGPT for schoolwork, double the share in 2023
sources.samplingMethod: Pew teens survey (details not yet verified in this audit)
limitations: NOT YET VERIFIED against the Pew page; value currently from secondary reporting (Boston Globe)
Asks about ChatGPT only, so it is not comparable to the 2025 'any chatbot' item
